subject: Food for thought from an interactive NYT graphic

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Food for thought from an interactive NYT graphic
parts:
I just saw this cool map showing the development of Manhattan's grid:
http://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2011/03/21/nyregion/map-of-how-manhattan-grid-grew.html

They did some interesting things that would be cool to have in some future version of ggplot. Even if it's not possible to implement them, I think it's useful to consider how various graphics could be described with the grammar of graphics.

First off, the map is interactive -- you can zoom and pan. This is sort of like using coord_cartesian and setting its parameters interactively with a mouse.

With the Street Openings overlay, there's a slider that lets you control what time-slice of the data is shown. It would be really nice to be able to specify a mapping like "slider=year", or something like that. With the Growth overlay, there are four different years that are clickable; you click on a year to see the census data from that year. Conceptually, these things let you interactively view a subset of the data. As far as I can tell, interactivity is something that can't be described very well with aesthetic mappings or with faceting.

Even the 1811 and 1836 overlay maps could be implemented with something this, using a geom_raster for the overlay map. However, instead of mapping a data value to the slider, you'd map alpha to the slider.

There are many practical issues with doing this, such as:
- Grid graphics doesn't have sliders or other interactive components (as far as I know)
- Most export formats don't support interaction (though maybe PDF does?)

Even so, it would be nice if the data structures in the new layers package could support interactive data presentation, even if the present rendering backend doesn't. 

Thoughts?

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Food for thought from an interactive NYT graphic
parts:
I think that the pieces already exist in various places, but the
question is how to coordinate them all in ggplot2. The NYT plot to
which you refer appears to be an example of a 'Hans Rosling plot',
basically a set of static plots of the same phenomenon with the same
x-y axis limits done over time and strung together with a slider. The
googleVis package provides one way to make these sorts of plots in R.

Two packages that seem relevant to this enterprise are animation and
RGoogleMaps. The NYT plot is done in GoogleVis, but I can't tell if
it's through R or not. In the googleVis package, you arrange the data
to make a call to googleVis, which then renders the (animated)
graphic. See the googleVis demo for some examples; the googleVis
package description provides a few more links. Michael Friendly did a
couple of googleVis plots in the Lahman package (see the examples
under the hitters data).

googleVis is self-contained - you feed the data and the plot call
function from the package and R communicates with the GoogleVis
application to produce the graphic. To do something similar with
ggplot2, one option would be to create a series of static plots and
then use the animate package to string them into a video display. I
seem to recall that a few people have used ggplot2 in conjunction with
RGoogleMaps to produce some neat displays, so perhaps some combination
of ggplot2, RGoogleMaps and animation would provide parallel
functionality to googleVis for graphs similar to the one referenced
here.

Heike Hoffman did some animation for the airlines data:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/Flying-over-the-usa
so this sort of thing has been done before with ggplot2, but I don't
think it's been systematized yet. See also
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/Crime-in-Downtown-Houston%2C-Texas-%3A-Combining-ggplot2-and-Google-Maps
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/Using-ggplot2-animations-to-demonstrate-several-parallel-numerical-experiments-in-a-single-layout

The use of sliders to handle time and zooming is another issue that
probably requires some means of adding interactivity to the package
and that's likely to be a nontrivial concern. I'll bet it's on
Hadley's long term radar screen, though, so I'm looking forward to his
take on this, as well as that of others.

Dennis

messages.author: d34d025a513c07fc
messages.subject: Re: Food for thought from an interactive NYT graphic
parts:
> If there is going to be development in that direction, please tell me
> how I can help out. Because I am very interested in that.

It would be really useful to see a few examples of common ggplot2
graphics (e.g. with facetting, various types of scales), rendered with
d3. You could start by turning the output of ggplot_build() into json.
That would help me understand the hurdles we'd need to overcome.

If you're serious about being able to export, I'd like to suggest a way of thinking about this. Instead of thinking about exporting the data for d3, we should consider providing a platform-agnostic description of the graph.

Here's the question to consider: What information is necessary to fully describe the desired output?  I think this should be the output of ggplot2_build, or some other function in the pipeline. This description could then be translated and rendered with a grid-based rendering system, as is currently done, or gridSVG, or even d3.

In order to answer the question, we need to specify the baseline capabilities of all drawing platforms that will be used to render the grpah (e.g., grid, gridSVG, and d3). Right now, ggplot2 is built around grid graphics. This means if the output of ggplot2_build() refers to grid-specific aesthetics like size, shape, and linetype, it can't be used by another drawing platform like d3, without hacking in how 'linetype' works in grid.

The procedure might be something like this:
1. start with data + ggplot specification 
2. use ggplot_build to generate platform-agnostic description of the graph (call it the PAD)
3. give the description to a drawing platform (e.g., a grid-based system or d3)


Each drawing platform may have capabilities beyond the baseline. For example, it looks like gridSVG's capabilities are a superset of grid's, and d3's capabilities may overlap with grid without being a super- or subset. And grid itself may have more capabilities than the baseline.

You could also allow use of extended capabilities of each drawing platform. For example, imagine that gridSVG supported a slider control. You could then give a PAD with sliders to a gridSVG-based platform and it would come out fine. But if you gave the same PAD to a grid-based platform, it would throw a warning or error.

If things all worked out this way, the PAD could used as a standard data interchange format -- it could be generated by something other than ggplot2 in R, and rendered by something other than ggplot2 in R.


All of that said, I realize that it may be totally impractical to completely abstract away from the individual drawing platforms. And there's a danger of going too far and building an entire graphics system when the payoff isn't large enough to warrant it. But, at the very least, this could be a useful tool for thinking about how to structure things.

Also, I agree that having real examples with d3 is a good idea, since it's always helpful to have something concrete to look at.

-Winston

messages.author: dc06d729e023580a
messages.subject: Re: Food for thought from an interactive NYT graphic
parts:
> If you're serious about being able to export, I'd like to suggest a way of
> thinking about this. Instead of thinking about exporting the data for d3, we
> should consider providing a platform-agnostic description of the graph.

I think that's a good way of thinking about the problem, but I think
we are not quite aligned on what the problem is. I think it's useful
to have a quick and dirty way of getting 90% of a ggplot2 graphic into
d3, to provide an easy base for further experimentation.

A bigger problem, is what's the best way to specify and render
interactive graphics? To best answer this question, my gut feeling is
you want to stick to one rendering system (e.g. grid OR d3) and
optimise the heck out of it. If you try and span multiple graphics
systems you end up with mediocrity.

Hadley
